title: A Name Nobody Chose
description: Where the word pagan came from, and why Europe's old religions reach us through outsiders

concepts.title: Paganus: Hick, Civilian or Outsider?
concepts.contentHtml:
The word pagan is a Christian label for outsiders, not a name that the worshippers of Jupiter, Woden or Perun used for themselves, and how it got its religious meaning is still argued over. Latin paganus comes from pagus, a country district. In the first century CE it had two everyday senses: a villager, and a civilian as opposed to a soldier.

Scholars have offered three explanations for the religious sense:

  • Rustic: the old cults supposedly lingered longest in the countryside, so Christians called their rivals country folk.
  • Civilian: Christians thought of themselves as soldiers of Christ (milites Christi), so an unbeliever was someone who had never enlisted.
  • Outsider: Mohrmann, writing in 1952, argued that "civilian" was one case of a broader sense, "outsider", so a paganus was simply anyone outside the Christian community.

The timeline is telling. Early Christians used biblical words such as gentiles and nationes instead, and they did not use paganus for non-Christians before the age of Constantine.1 Its first official use in the religious sense is a law of 370, and it caught on almost universally in the fifth century, just as the thing it described was dying out.

In 1977 the classicist James J. O'Donnell spotted a pattern. Augustine used the word freely when writing to fellow Christians, but almost never in The City of God, a work meant to persuade pagan readers. O'Donnell suggested the word carried a sneer: it let Christians call even rich, cultured senators "hicks" behind their backs.2 Whatever its origin, it was never a name its bearers chose.

concepts.title: Gods in Roman Dress
concepts.contentHtml:
The first detailed descriptions of northern Europe's gods were written by Romans, and Romans saw foreign gods through their own. Julius Caesar, writing about the Gauls he was conquering, reported that they worshipped "Mercury" above all, as the inventor of all arts and the guide of travellers, followed by Apollo, Mars, Jupiter and Minerva. He gives no Gaulish names at all. In 98 CE Tacitus said the Germans also chiefly worshipped Mercury, sometimes with human victims, and appeased Hercules and Mars with animal offerings.

Tacitus even shows the habit at work. Describing an ancient grove of the Naharvali, whose priest dressed like a woman, he says that by the Roman explanation the gods there were Castor and Pollux, though the locals called the divinity the Alcis. Scholars call this habit interpretatio romana, the Roman reading of foreign gods. Like any translation it lost things. A Roman reader learned which job a god seemed to do, not what its own worshippers said about it.

The habit ran both ways. People living under Roman rule, Roman soldiers among them, set up altars to paired names such as Sulis Minerva, the goddess of the hot spring at Bath, and to local mother goddesses under a Latin title, such as the Matronae Austriahenae of Morken-Harff in the Rhineland, whose altar was found in 1958. So "Mercury" in a Roman text might be an outsider's guess, or an equation that worshippers made themselves.

Telling the two apart is one of the first problems anyone studying Europe's old religions has to face, and you will meet it in every lesson of this topic.

concepts.title: Written by Those Who Tore Them Down
concepts.contentHtml:
After the Romans came Christian writers, who had even stronger reasons to describe the old gods badly. As the scholar Marija Gimbutas warned about the Slavs, our descriptions of their idols and temples come from the writings of the very people who destroyed them.1 The Russian Primary Chronicle, the main source for the gods of Kyiv, was compiled around 1111, more than a century after those idols fell. The pattern repeats across Europe: Bede on the Anglo-Saxons, Saxo Grammaticus on the Baltic Slavs, churchmen of the seventeenth century on the Balts.

Historians therefore work with four kinds of evidence, each with its own trap:

  • Classical outsiders such as Caesar and Tacitus: early, but filtered through Roman categories and the politics of conquest.
  • Christian writers: often closer to the people, but usually hostile and writing after the event.
  • Archaeology: shrines, offerings and bodies that are real but silent, so their meaning has to be inferred.
  • Later folklore: songs and customs written down centuries later, which may preserve old ideas or may have been reshaped.

The Baltic peoples show how slippery the last category can be. Their folk songs and tales are among the richest in Europe, yet the Encyclopedia of Religion's survey of Baltic religion notes that the national awakening of the late nineteenth century brought a tendency to create pseudo-gods and figments of imagination, as patriots searched for ancient precedents. Folklore can carry the past, but it can also be made to order.

The rest of this topic follows these four strands, and keeps asking of every claim: who wrote this, when, and why?

title: Gods at Home
description: Hearth rites, household shrines, bargains with the gods and the curse tablets of Roman Bath

concepts.title: The Hearth and the Cupboard Shrine
concepts.contentHtml:
Temples and state festivals were only part of ancient religion. Many offerings were made at home, by ordinary families, every day. (Rome's state cults are covered in Gods That Died and the initiation cults in Mysteries & Hidden Faiths; this lesson stays in the kitchen.)

In a Greek house the centre was the hearth, sacred to Hestia. Often it was only a portable brazier, but it stood for the heart of the household. A newborn baby was carried around it, and brides and newly arrived slaves were showered with nuts and figs in front of it.1 At everyday meals a token morsel might be thrown into the fire for the goddess. Hestia also received the first and last libations at a feast, which gave the Greeks a saying: "to begin from Hestia".

A Roman family kept its gods in a lararium, a cupboard-shrine usually in the atrium, holding statuettes of the Lares, guardian spirits of the family, alongside the Penates, spirits of the store cupboard. The head of the household led the rites. Before a meal the family gave thanks and set aside a portion to burn in the hearth, and the household genius, often shown as a snake, was honoured on the master's birthday. When a family moved house, its Lares and Penates moved with it. Whole neighbourhoods honoured Lares of the crossroads at the festival of the Compitalia.

All this was religion as an exchange. In the writer Antony Kamm's summary, Roman faith was less a spiritual experience than a contractual relationship between people and the forces that controlled their lives. Feed the household gods and the household would thrive; neglect them and it would suffer.

concepts.title: A Bargain with the Gods
concepts.contentHtml:
Much ancient prayer was a promise with a condition attached. A Roman made a vow (votum): help me, and I will give you something. When the god delivered, the worshipper paid up, often with a stone altar carved with the letters V S L M, short for votum solvit libens merito, "fulfilled the vow willingly and deservedly". At Bath a freedman called Aufidius Eutuches set up such an altar to the goddess Sulis for the welfare and safety of his former master, a centurion of the Sixth Legion.1

Healing sanctuaries show the same logic in clay. At the sanctuary of the healing god Asclepius in Corinth, excavations in the 1920s and 1930s turned up more than 900 fragments of terracotta body parts: legs, arms, feet, ears, eyes, breasts and genitals. These anatomical votives were offered by people asking for a cure or giving thanks for one. Some look made to order rather than mass-produced: one hand shows what may be an abscess, and some ears have holes pierced for real earrings.

The impulse has outlived the gods it once served. In Canindé, in north-eastern Brazil, Catholic pilgrims to St Francis still leave milagres, often models of the body part that was healed, as the sign of a promise kept, and the American anthropologist Lindsey King has interviewed them about why. That makes the Brazilian shrine a useful comparison for archaeologists, who cannot interview anyone at Corinth.

Notice what this does and does not show. A practice can look almost unchanged across two thousand years while the beliefs behind it change completely. Continuity of practice is not continuity of religion, a distinction this topic will return to in its final lesson.

concepts.title: Curses for Stolen Gloves
concepts.contentHtml:
Sometimes the bargain turned nasty. A curse tablet (defixio, from defigere, "to fix") was a thin sheet of lead inscribed with a request that a god act against someone. By the late 1980s more than 1,500 were known, two-thirds of them in Greek. Ancient writers rarely mention them, but one famous case stands out: when the Roman prince Germanicus lay dying at Antioch in AD 19, his room reportedly held lead tablets with his name scratched on them.

In 1979 and 1980 excavators at the sacred spring of Sulis in Bath recovered 130 tablets, one of the largest groups ever published.1 Almost all deal with petty theft. A man named Docimedis had lost two gloves (or perhaps sleeves; the Latin word is almost unique) and asked that the thief should lose his mind and his eyes in the goddess's temple. Others had lost cloaks, a bracelet, a silver ring, small sums of money and even a ploughshare. Fifteen tablets formally "give" the stolen goods, or the thief, to Sulis, making recovery her business. The tablets' editor described the goddess as being treated like a debt-enforcement agency, or a supernatural detective.

Britain turns out to be odd. Elsewhere in the Greco-Roman world, curse tablets mostly target slanderers, opponents in lawsuits, rivals in love and racing charioteers; among about 1,300 known from outside Britain, only some twenty were prompted by theft. In Britain almost every tablet that can be classified is aimed at a thief.

The authors were not rich. They carried much less cash than the second-century legionaries who lost purses while building Hadrian's Wall, and the editor concluded that they came from a lower social and economic stratum. These tablets are among the rare first-person voices of ordinary provincials, and they show religion doing a practical job.

title: The Druids: Evidence and Invention
description: What Caesar, Pliny and Tacitus reported, what archaeology adds, and how the druids were reinvented

concepts.title: Caesar's Druids
concepts.contentHtml:
Almost everything written about the ancient druids comes from Greek and Roman authors, and one of the fullest accounts is by a general at war with their people. In Book 6 of his Gallic War, Julius Caesar describes two ranks of Gauls who mattered: the knights, who fought, and the druids, who conducted public and private sacrifices and interpreted all matters of religion.

His druids are far more than priests. They judge murders, inheritance disputes and boundary quarrels, and anyone who defies them is barred from the sacrifices, which Caesar calls the heaviest punishment among the Gauls. They pay no tax and do not go to war. One chief druid presides, and they meet each year at a consecrated place in the land of the Carnutes, reckoned the centre of Gaul. Caesar adds that the system was believed to have been invented in Britain, and that keen students still went there to learn it.

Two details are often repeated. Training could last twenty years, because pupils memorised great numbers of verses. The druids thought it wrong to write their teachings down, although the Gauls used Greek letters for ordinary business.1 Caesar guessed at two reasons: they did not want their doctrine spread among the common people, and they did not want pupils to lean on writing and neglect their memories. The druids also taught that souls do not die but pass from one body to another, which Caesar thought made men fearless in battle.

Notice what this means for you as a historian. Because the druids refused to write, no druidic scripture, hymn or prayer survives at all. Caesar's account is precious, but it is a conqueror's description written for Roman readers, and every later picture of the druids, ancient or modern, is built on a handful of passages like this one.

concepts.title: Mistletoe, Wicker and the Groves of Mona
concepts.contentHtml:
The best-loved druid image comes from Pliny the Elder (23 to 79 CE). The druids, he says, hold nothing more sacred than mistletoe growing on an oak. Beneath the tree they prepare a sacrifice and a feast and bring two white bulls; a priest in white climbs up, cuts the mistletoe with a golden hook1 (the "golden sickle" of later retellings) and catches it on a white cloak. The plant should be gathered, if possible, on the sixth day of the moon.

The darkest image comes from Caesar. The Gauls, he says, believed that only a human life could buy a human life, and some built figures of vast size from wicker, filled them with living men and set them alight. Thieves and robbers were the preferred victims, but when there were not enough, the innocent were used. Strabo described a similar giant figure stuffed with cattle, wild animals and people. And when Roman troops attacked the island of Mona (Anglesey) in the year of Boudica's revolt, Tacitus describes women in black robes with flaming torches running between the ranks, and a circle of druids lifting their hands to heaven and calling down curses. The Romans won, then cut down the sacred groves, because, Tacitus says, the islanders consulted their gods using human entrails.

How much should you believe? These writers were the druids' enemies, and Roman distaste for human sacrifice was one reason emperors such as Tiberius and Claudius tried to wipe druidism out. The wider evidence points to offerings of animals and weapons among Iron Age Celtic peoples and, much more rarely, of people. It cannot tell us who did the killing, or confirm the wicker giants. Human sacrifice probably happened; the vivid details come from outsiders with a case to make.

concepts.title: Stonehenge, Primrose Hill and a Forged Tradition
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask what druids are famous for and many people will say Stonehenge. The dates rule it out. English Heritage dates the first earthwork there to about 3000 BCE and the great stone circle to about 2500 BCE, thousands of years before druids appear in any written record. The link was made by antiquaries. In the late seventeenth century John Aubrey concluded that stone circles were built by native Britons rather than Romans or Danes, and since the druids were the only prehistoric British priests named in classical texts, he credited them with Stonehenge.1 In 1740 William Stukeley published Stonehenge, a Temple Restor'd to the British Druids, and the idea stuck.

Modern druid ceremony owes even more to one man. Iolo Morganwg (Edward Williams, 1747 to 1826), a stonemason from Glamorgan, claimed that druidism had survived in its purest form in his home county and that he was its heir. One of his most accomplished forgeries was probably written during a year in a Cardiff debtors' prison. On 21 June 1792 he held the first Gorsedd of the Bards of the Island of Britain on Primrose Hill in London, inside a small circle of stones, tying green, blue and white ribbons on the arms of new members. Many of his forgeries were published in 1801 and 1807 as copies of old manuscripts, and an edition of the medieval poet Dafydd ap Gwilym that he published in 1789 included poems Iolo had written himself.

His forgeries were not exposed until the twentieth century, by the scholar Griffith John Williams. By then the Gorsedd had become a much-loved part of the National Eisteddfod of Wales, and it still is: since 2004 its circle has used realistic fake stones so that it can stand on the Eisteddfod field. An invented tradition can become a real one.

title: Gifts to the Water
description: Bog bodies, lake hoards, and how archaeologists decide that something was a ritual

concepts.title: Tollund Man's Last Meal
concepts.contentHtml:
On 8 May 1950 peat cutters in a Danish bog near Silkeborg uncovered a man so well preserved that they suspected a crime and called the police. He lay on his side as if asleep, naked except for a pointed sheepskin cap and a hide belt, with stubble on his chin. Around his neck was a tightly tied leather strap, coiled over his shoulder and down his back. Tollund Man had been hanged and then carefully laid in the bog with his eyes closed. Recent research puts his death around 400 BCE, though an older radiocarbon date pointed nearer 220 BCE.

His burial was unusual for its time and place: people in the region normally cremated their dead and placed the ashes in cemeteries. Another hanged body, the Elling Girl, had been found in 1938 only 61 metres away. Estimates of the number of bog bodies found in north-western Europe run as high as 2,000, most from about 500 BCE to 100 CE, and many show violent deaths.

In 2021 a team led by Nina Nielsen of Museum Silkeborg re-examined his gut contents. His last meal, eaten 12 to 24 hours before death, was barley porridge with seeds of pale persicaria and flax, probably with fish, cooked in a clay pot. The weed seeds, sand and charcoal suggest threshing waste swept up from the floor went into the pot. Was that a special meal for a victim, or ordinary Iron Age cooking? The researchers could not say. The meal was nutritious, so they found no sign of a famine that might explain a sacrifice.1 He also had whipworm, tapeworm and mawworm.

Tollund Man is usually interpreted as a sacrifice, but notice how that conclusion is built: from the care taken with his body, the contrast with normal burial, and the bog as a place of offerings. No text from Iron Age Denmark tells us why he died.

concepts.title: Lindow Man: Sacrifice, Execution or Murder?
concepts.contentHtml:
Britain's best-known bog body surfaced on a conveyor belt. On 1 August 1984 a worker at a peat company on Lindow Moss in Cheshire pulled off what looked like a lump of wood; when it hit the ground, the peat fell away to reveal a human leg. The remains went first to a hospital mortuary, because local police were investigating a murder. The year before, a woman's skull had come out of the same bog, and a local suspect whose house backed onto the moss confessed to killing his wife. Then a radiocarbon date showed that the skull was about 1,800 years old.

Lindow Man was about 25, with a beard clipped with shears. He had taken blows to the head and the back, had been garrotted with a thin cord, and had his throat cut.1 Radiocarbon dates place his death between about 2 BCE and 129 CE, as Iron Age Britain was becoming Roman Britannia. His gut held cereal food and traces of mistletoe pollen.

This "triple death" invited a dramatic reading. Ross and Robins (1989) linked it to the appeasement of three Celtic gods by ritual sacrifice, pointing to the mistletoe that Pliny connected with druids. Others were cautious: the pollen specialist Scaife suggested the mistletoe was more likely medicinal, and Current Archaeology's Neil Faulkner has openly asked whether the ritual interpretation is right at all.

Tacitus offers another possibility. Among the Germans, he says, traitors and deserters were hanged on trees, while cowards and men stained with abominable vices were plunged into a bog with a hurdle put over them. A body in a bog might be a gift to the gods, an executed criminal or a murder victim, and the physical evidence alone does not always decide which.

concepts.title: Hoards in the Lake and the Ritual Label
concepts.contentHtml:
Bodies are rare; objects are everywhere. On 28 May 1891 peat cutters near Gundestrup in Jutland found a silver cauldron 69 centimetres across, taken apart into its plates and laid in a bog. The Gundestrup cauldron, now in the National Museum of Denmark, is covered with gods, warriors and a sacrifice of bulls, but its silverwork and its elephants and griffins point to the lower Danube, in Thrace or Dacia. Two historians call it "not Celtic, or, at least, not just Celtic".

In the 1940s, work to extend the airfield of RAF Valley on Anglesey brought up an Iron Age treasure from a lake, Llyn Cerrig Bach: over 150 iron and bronze objects from between about 300 BCE and 100 CE, including weapons, chariot fittings, cauldrons and slave chains with neck collars. In 2024 service personnel and veterans digging there found more, including a bridle-bit and a terret ring for chariot reins. Caesar had described the same habit in Gaul: after a victory, captured spoils were heaped up in consecrated places, and almost no one dared to take them.

How do archaeologists decide a deposit was ritual, rather than lost, hidden or thrown away? Since a brief 1984 study of Neolithic material by Richards and Thomas, many have looked for structured deposition: particular objects placed in particular contexts in a patterned way. Critics note that the words used for such finds (placed, special, odd, token, symbolic) run together different ideas, and Chadwick has asked whether rubbish disposal and deliberate placing can be told apart at all.1 A careful test compares a suspect deposit with the ordinary background of finds across a site. Even then, preservation can mislead: a yew bucket and an ash spade from a late Roman well near Leeds may look special only because waterlogged ground preserved what usually rots.

title: Woden's England and the Felled Oaks
description: Nerthus, Eostre, gods in English place names, and missionaries who kept or felled the shrines

concepts.title: Nerthus in Her Curtained Wagon
concepts.contentHtml:
The earliest glimpse of the gods of the English comes from Rome. In 98 CE Tacitus wrote the Germania, a short account of the Germanic peoples. He names seven northern tribes, the Angli among them, who shared a cult of Nerthus, "Mother Earth". On an island in the ocean stood a sacred grove holding a wagon covered with a cloth, which only her priest could touch. When the priest sensed the goddess was present, the wagon was drawn through the land by cows, and wherever she went there was feasting and peace: no one went to war and every weapon was locked away until she returned to her temple.

Then the wagon, the cloth and, "if you choose to believe it", the goddess herself were washed in a secret lake by slaves, who were then drowned in the same lake. Tacitus says this filled everyone with a mysterious terror and a holy ignorance about a sight that only those about to die could see.

How far can you trust this? Tacitus filtered northern peoples through Roman eyes, as the first lesson showed: he also says the Germans' chief god was "Mercury". The scholar Richard North notes that the name Nerthus matches that of the later Norse god Njörðr, and suggests that Tacitus may have mistaken a divine husband and wife for a single earth goddess.1 The bogs of northern Europe hold the bodies you met in the last lesson, so drowned attendants are not far-fetched, but no find can be tied to Nerthus by name.

After the Angles, Saxons and others settled in Britain, they stayed pagan until various points in the seventh century. What they believed is hard to know, because the evidence is scraps: place names, royal genealogies and passages in mostly Latin Christian works.

concepts.title: Woden in the Landscape, Eostre in the Calendar
concepts.contentHtml:
The days of the week still honour Tiw, Woden, Thor and Frigg, as Gods That Died explains. Place names add a map. The gods' names Woden, Tiw and Thunor (the English Thor), and perhaps a goddess called Freo, survive in English place names, but only in the south and the Midlands, and Woden's is the commonest. His name also appears in eighth-century Anglian royal genealogies. Other Old English place-name elements show where worship happened: weoh marked a wayside shrine and hearh a public one, though archaeologists find such shrines hard to recognise in excavated ground plans.

Then there is Eostre. In his works on calculating the church year, the Northumbrian monk Bede (about 675 to 735) wrote that his heathen ancestors had held a festival for a goddess named Eostre at about the time of year when Christians mark Christ's Passion. Because the English word Easter comes from the same root, the claim is endlessly repeated as "Easter is named after a pagan goddess".

Bede is the only witness, and scholars disagree about him. Richard North points out that nothing outside Bede suggests a personified goddess, and argues that Bede may have turned a seasonal word into a deity by analogy with Februus, a Roman god Bede knew to be associated with February.1 In Bede's favour, he wrote within about a century of his people's conversion, so he was not far removed from the pagan past.

Either way, the dispute concerns one word. Even if Eostre was a real goddess, the English name of the feast is no evidence that Easter's customs came from her worship.

concepts.title: Keep the Temples, Fell the Oak
concepts.contentHtml:
Missionaries disagreed about what to do with pagan holy places. In 601 Pope Gregory the Great sent a letter after the abbot Mellitus, preserved by Bede, with surprising advice for the English mission: destroy the idols but keep the temples,1 sprinkle them with holy water, set up altars and relics, so that people would keep coming to places they knew. Since the English were used to slaughtering oxen in sacrifice, let them build huts of branches around the new churches on saints' days and feast there, killing cattle to the praise of God instead. Yet in a letter Bede places at the same time, Gregory urged King Æthelberht of Kent to suppress the worship of idols and overthrow the structures of the temples.

Bede also tells a conversion story from the inside. In 627, as King Edwin weighed the new faith, his chief priest Coifi declared the old religion useless. A high priest was forbidden to carry weapons or ride anything but a mare, so Coifi asked for arms and the king's stallion, rode to the temple at Goodmanham near York and hurled a spear into it, while onlookers thought he had gone mad. Then he had the temple and its enclosures burned.

On the Continent the approach was blunter. In Hesse, according to his biographer Willibald, the missionary Boniface, with the support of local converts, took an axe to an enormous oak at Geismar that the pagans called the Oak of Jupiter, a tree associated with the thunder god Donar. It crashed down, split into four, and Boniface built a chapel from its timber. In 772 Charlemagne's army destroyed the Irminsul, a sacred pillar of the Saxons, at the start of more than thirty years of war, and his ordinances for Saxony made pagan practice punishable by death.

title: The Last Pagans of Europe
description: Perun in the Dnieper, the four-headed god of Arkona, Lithuania's late baptism and the Sámi drums

concepts.title: Perun Goes into the Dnieper
concepts.contentHtml:
In 980, says the Russian Primary Chronicle, Prince Vladimir of Kyiv set up idols on a hill outside his palace: a wooden Perun with a head of silver and a mouth of gold, together with Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl and Mokosh. It is the only Slavic pantheon on record from the East Slavic lands. Perun was a thunder god. In the sixth century the Byzantine historian Procopius had heard of Slavs who worshipped a thunder god as "lord of the whole world", and in the tenth century princes of Kyiv swore to their treaties with Byzantium by Perun's name.

Eight years later Vladimir cast down his own idols and had the people of Kyiv baptised by force. The Chronicle describes the scene with relish. Some idols were cut to pieces and others burned. Perun was tied to a horse's tail and dragged down to the stream, and twelve men were appointed to beat him with sticks, not because the wood could feel it, the Chronicle explains, but to insult the demon who had deceived people in that form.1 As the idol was dragged towards the Dnieper the unbelievers wept over it, and then it was thrown into the river.

Two cautions apply. The Chronicle was compiled around 1111 by Christian writers, more than a century later, and it tells a triumphant story. And the old god did not vanish so neatly. In folk religion Perun merged with St Elijah (Il'ia), who crosses the heavens in a chariot in Russian icons, and a bull sacrifice with a communal feast on St Il'ia's Day was recorded in northern Russia as late as 1907.

concepts.title: Arkona and the Four-Headed God
concepts.contentHtml:
Among the Slavs of the southern Baltic coast, in what is now Germany, the old religion was organised around rich temples and held out into the twelfth century. Most of what we know comes from churchmen on the other side, such as Bishop Thietmar of Merseburg, the biographers of Bishop Otto of Bamberg, and the Danish historian Saxo Grammaticus.

The best-documented site is Arkona, a temple-fortress on the island of Rügen sacred to the god Sventovit. According to Saxo, the temple was a red-roofed timber building of fine workmanship, inside a carved and painted wooden fence with a single entrance. In its inner chamber stood a statue of Sventovit, larger than life, with four heads facing the four cardinal directions. In 1168 Christian Danes stormed Rügen and destroyed it.1 Saxo also describes the temples of nearby Garz, where an oak statue of Rugievit had seven heads, seven swords hanging at its belt and an eighth in its hand.

Is Saxo exaggerating? Here archaeology helps. Carl Schuchhardt's excavation in 1921 proved that the temple at Arkona existed, and digs in 1969 and 1970 found an earlier layer of the sanctuary going back to the tenth century, possibly the ninth. Far to the east, near Novgorod, archaeologists in 1951 found at a place called Peryn the octagonal, rosette-shaped floor plan of what may have been a temple of Perun, with charcoal at its centre where an idol and a fire probably stood.

When text and spade agree, historians can speak with more confidence. But notice the division of labour: the excavation can confirm a building, while only Saxo's hostile text tells you the god had four heads.

concepts.title: Lithuania's Late Baptism and the Sámi Drums
concepts.contentHtml:
The Lithuanians accepted Christianity, in Pope John Paul II's words, "some centuries after" their neighbours. Squeezed between Slavic powers to the east and the crusading Teutonic Knights to the west, they long resisted, as the pope put it in 1987, "accepting the Cross from those who came against them with the sword". Grand Duke Mindaugas accepted baptism and a crown from Pope Innocent IV in 1251, but his people did not follow, and his death in 1263 ended the experiment. In 1386 Grand Duke Jogaila agreed to be baptised, and with it gained the crown of Poland and Queen Jadwiga's hand. In 1387 he returned to Vilnius and set a mass baptism in motion, and the western region of Samogitia was evangelised from 1413. Their Baltic cousins the Old Prussians, conquered during German eastward expansion, had disappeared as a people by the seventeenth century.

In the far north, the Sámi kept their own religion longer still. A noaidi, a religious specialist, used a drum of reindeer skin painted with the Sámi world to enter trances, travel to other realms and foretell events. In 1609 King Christian IV of Denmark and Norway made drum use a crime punishable by death.1 In 1692 the noaidi Anders Poulsen, tried for witchcraft at Vadsø, played his drum in court and explained how it eased women in labour and found stolen goods; a jailor killed him before any verdict. His drum ended up in the National Museum of Denmark. It has been displayed at the Sámi museum in Karasjok since 1979, and in January 2022 Denmark transferred its ownership there. About 71 old Sámi drums are known to survive.

title: Survival or Reinvention?
description: Maypoles, Christmas trees, the witch-cult theory and the modern pagans who rebuild old faiths

concepts.title: Are Maypoles and Christmas Trees Pagan?
concepts.contentHtml:
Many seasonal customs are said to be pagan survivals. Check the evidence and the story usually becomes more interesting. (The 25 December question is covered in Gods That Died, and Easter's name in lesson 5.)

The maypole was already being denounced as an idol in 1583, when the Puritan Phillip Stubbes described villagers hauling one home behind twenty or forty yoke of oxen and called it "this stinkyng ydol". That was a Puritan insult, not a historian's finding, but it stuck. Much of the maypole you picture is newer still. Early maypoles were decked with flowers, and dancers held hands in a ring; the first documented maypole with plaited ribbons appeared on a stage,1 in the play Richard Plantagenet at London's Victoria Theatre (now the Old Vic) in 1836. The ribbon dance was copied across the country, and Victorian schools spread the crowning of May Queens.

The Christmas tree has a similar story. Romans decked their homes with evergreens at the New Year, and the theologian Tertullian scolded Christians who did the same. But clear records of trees as a Christmas symbol begin only in the sixteenth century, in Latvia in 1510 (a disputed claim) and Strasbourg in 1521, and the first detailed description, of a Strasbourg tree hung with paper roses, dates from 1605. One plausible theory links such trees to the "paradise trees" hung with fruit in medieval plays, since Christmas Eve was also the feast of Adam and Eve. The legend that Martin Luther invented the tree has little historical basis. The tale that Boniface pointed converts to a fir after felling the oak at Geismar is also only a legend: in Willibald's account he builds a chapel from the oak's timber. The tree became common in England only in the nineteenth century, popularised by Queen Victoria.

concepts.title: Frazer, Murray and the Survival Machine
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do so many people assume old customs are pagan? Partly because of two hugely influential books. In The Golden Bough (first edition 1890), the anthropologist James George Frazer gathered May trees, harvest rites and midsummer fires from all over Europe and read them as "relics of tree worship", traces of prehistoric fertility beliefs that had survived among peasants. The method was to collect similar-looking customs and assume a common ancient root. It was thrilling, and very hard to test.

In 1921 the Egyptologist Margaret Murray, who by 1914 was effectively running the Egyptology department at University College London, pushed the idea much further in The Witch-Cult in Western Europe, published by Oxford University Press. Seizing on some unusual testimony from sixteenth-century Scottish witch trials, she argued that what people called witchcraft was really the last trace of a fertility cult going back to the Neolithic, practised in covens of thirteen who worshipped a horned god mistaken for the devil. The few specialists in the history of witchcraft dismissed it: she relied on a narrow set of hostile records, some extracted under torture. But Murray wrote the Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on witchcraft, became president of the Folklore Society, and in 1954 argued that every major political assassination in English history had been a ritual sacrifice.

Historians of witchcraft have long since rejected the witch-cult theory,1 and with it the idea of an organised pagan religion surviving in secret. Murray's ideas did help inspire Gerald Gardner's Wicca (covered in Western Esotericism), yet the historian Francis Young notes that few Wiccans and neopagans now believe literally that their religion has existed since prehistory. The lesson is one of method: a resemblance between two customs is a question to investigate, not evidence of descent.

concepts.title: Rebuilding the Old Gods
concepts.contentHtml:
If the old religions did not survive in secret, today's pagan religions are revivals, and their founders have often said so openly. In 1925 the Latvian artist Ernests Brastiņš and a colleague published a manifesto called The Restoration of Latvian Religion, and in 1926 their community of Dievturi ("those who keep their God") was registered as a religious organisation. Brastiņš built doctrine and ritual from mythology and folk songs, and counted years from a supposed dawn of the Indo-Europeans about 10,000 years earlier, so that 1926 became 11926. After the Soviet occupation he was deported and shot in a Russian prison in 1942; the movement survived in exile, above all in the United States.

In Lithuania, Romuva was revived in 1967 as an association for the study of local culture, organising midsummer celebrations. It was dissolved in 1971 after accusations of nationalism and religious activity, re-emerged in 1988, and was registered in 1992 as the Community of Baltic Faith Romuva. Its central ideas are darna, harmony, and dora, respect for all life. In England and Wales, the Charity Commission registered The Druid Network as a charity on 21 September 2010, accepting that its reverence for nature as sacred amounted to a religion in charity law.1 Hellenic polytheists, Rodnovers and heathens are covered in Gods That Died.

Practitioners describe their own continuity in different ways, and often in more than one way at once. The Druid Network's constitution calls Druidry an ancient pagan religion, yet also describes modern Druidry as a spiritual relationship with the spirits of nature, landscape and ancestry. Whether a revived god is the same god is a question of faith, not history. What history can show is how each revival was made, and that the making is itself part of Europe's religious story.
